===== ORIGINAL PROMPT (initial_prompt.md) =====
Build a polished, fully offline iOS trip-planning app called "Waypoint".
Native Apple stack only: SwiftUI + SwiftData for persistence, MapKit for
all mapping, ActivityKit for Live Activities, EventKit for calendar
export. No backend, no accounts, no third-party SDKs, no network calls
except on-device MapKit/local geocoding (which works offline-cached but
may need network for tile fetch — if a feature would require live
network for correctness, don't fake it; record it as a gap). Follow the
ios-app-factory-rules.

Core features (complete over broad — ship fewer things fully working):

1. Trips & itinerary: create trips with a date range; each trip has
   multiple days; each day has an ordered list of stops (place name,
   address, optional MapKit-resolved coordinate, time window, notes,
   category icon). Reorder stops via drag-and-drop within a day AND
   across days. Get date math right across the trip's date range,
   including a trip that starts and ends on the same day and a
   single-day trip.

2. Map view: a MapKit view per day showing all of that day's stops as
   annotations connected by a route line (MKDirections walking/driving,
   gracefully degrading to a straight-line polyline with a visible
   "approximate" indicator if MKDirections has no network). Tapping a
   stop centers the map and highlights it; tapping a map pin selects
   the corresponding itinerary row (two-way binding).

3. Expense splitting: a per-trip list of travelers (name, no accounts).
   Log expenses (amount, payer, split method: equal / exact amounts /
   percentage) against any subset of travelers. A settle-up screen
   computing the minimum set of payments to zero every balance (the
   classic debt-simplification graph problem — get this genuinely
   correct, including rounding remainders so amounts always sum
   exactly). Use Decimal, never Double, for money.

4. Packing lists: per-trip checklist, templates the user can save and
   reapply to future trips, a "packed %" indicator.

5. Live Activity: while a trip is "active" (today falls within its date
   range), a Live Activity / Dynamic Island showing the current or next
   stop and time until it, updating as stops are checked off. Must
   degrade gracefully (no crash, no Live Activity) on devices/OS
   versions without support, and when the user denies the permission.

6. Calendar export: export a day's stops as EventKit calendar events
   (with the user's explicit permission), one event per stop honoring
   its time window; must not create duplicate events if exported twice
   for the same day — detect and either skip or update existing ones.

7. Home-screen widget (WidgetKit, separate target): shows the active
   trip's next stop, or "no active trip" honestly if none.

8. iPad: itinerary list and map must work as a genuine two-column split
   view on iPad, not just a stretched phone layout.

Priorities: the debt-simplification math, the drag-reorder data
integrity (no duplicate/lost stops across days), and honest degradation
of every system-permission-gated feature (Live Activities, Calendar,
location) — never fake success when a permission is denied or a
capability is unavailable in the Simulator. Explicitly call out in a
Gaps section anything requiring infrastructure this project can't
provide (live traffic data, real-time flight tracking, iCloud trip
sync). Seed a "demo trip" toggle in Settings with realistic multi-day
sample data so no screen is empty on first review. Provide a clear way
to run it in the iOS Simulator via Xcode.

  rationale: Retrofitting atomicity onto an already-built naive delete-then-insert implementation, or replacing a stubbed settle-up screen later, is far more expensive than building both correctly from the start, and this project's credibility rests specifically on these two mechanisms being genuinely correct rather than demo-plausible.
  rejected: Building a simpler placeholder version of drag-reorder or settlement first and hardening it in a later pass
  constraints: Directly extends DEC-prompt_contract-002, DEC-prompt_contract-003, and DEC-prompt_contract-005 into this slice's initial implementation, not a later hardening pass

- [[REDACTED:high_entropy]] Shrinking a trip's date range that would orphan stops on removed days must block the edit and show exactly which days/stops are affected, requiring the user to move or delete them first; extending the range is unrestricted.

  constraints: Applies to any trip date-range edit, not just drag operations; Must surface the specific affected stops, not just a generic warning
- [[REDACTED:high_entropy]] Expense entries using percentage splits that don't sum to 100% are rejected at entry with an inline validation error; the app never silently auto-rescales entered percentages.
  rationale: Silent rescaling would quietly reinterpret what the user typed, producing a different settle-up total than the numbers actually entered — directly violating the project's no-fake-success/no-silent-reinterpretation principle.

  constraints: Error message should state the actual sum so the user can correct it
- [[REDACTED:high_entropy]] A non-gesture 'Move to...' reorder action (context menu or edit-mode control) must exist alongside drag-and-drop, executing through the identical atomic SwiftData operation as the drag path.
  rationale: Drag gestures are not reliably operable via VoiceOver; without a parallel accessible path exercising the same atomic operation, a meaningful portion of users cannot reorder stops at all, and a divergent second implementation risks reintroducing the exact duplication bug the drag path is designed to prevent.
  rejected: Drag-only reordering with no accessible alternative; A separate, independently-implemented accessible reorder code path
  constraints: Both entry points (drag and Move-to) must call the same underlying atomic operation, not parallel implementations
- [[REDACTED:high_entropy]] The demo trip is a singleton keyed by a stable identifier: toggling it on creates the trip only if absent, toggling it off deletes exactly that trip and never touches any other trip.
  rationale: Without a singleton rule, repeated on/off/on toggling could create duplicate demo trips, which is either a confusing UX bug or a subtle data-integrity failure masquerading as a feature.
  rejected: Inserting a fresh demo trip on every toggle-on with no dedup
  constraints: Deletion on toggle-off must key off the stable identifier, never off name/date matching, so it can never delete a real user trip that happens to resemble it
- [[REDACTED:high_entropy]] All stop times are stored and displayed in the device's current local timezone; true destination-timezone-aware itineraries are explicitly out of scope and named as a Gap.

  rejected: Storing/interpreting stop times in the trip's origin timezone regardless of device location; Leaving timezone behavior undefined and letting it fall out of implementation choices
  constraints: Must be listed explicitly in the app's Gaps section per the original prompt's requirement
- [[REDACTED:high_entropy]] The debug/demo current-date injection hook (DEC-prompt_contract-009) must be wrapped in #if DEBUG and physically excluded from release builds, not merely gated behind a settings flag.

  rejected: Gating the hook behind a settings toggle only, left compiled into release builds
  constraints: Applies to the testability mechanism introduced in DEC-prompt_contract-009 specifically

  rejected: Leaving any token as a descriptive adjective for the build phase to interpret

- [DEC-design_handoff-002] Navigation is a single NavigationStack (iPhone)/NavigationSplitView (iPad) rooted at the trip switcher, never a tab bar; the iPad two-pane split (itinerary/map) activates only inside the day view, not app-wide.

  constraints: EmptyStateCard specifically must be the single implementation reused everywhere an empty state appears

  constraints: Build-verification must confirm all listed states are individually reachable and visually distinct, not just coded as a shared component with text swaps

  constraints: Applies specifically to the interactions named; screens without narrative weight keep system-default transitions

# First-Party Apple Frameworks Cheatsheet (iOS 17+ / Swift 5.9+)

Build capable iPhone apps with **zero third-party dependencies**. For each framework: when to reach for it, the entry-point type, and a compilable, idiomatic snippet or the gotcha that bites people. All examples target **iOS 17 minimum** unless a call-out says otherwise; Swift Concurrency (`async`/`await`) is preferred over completion handlers everywhere Apple offers it.

## General rules

- **Prefer these over SPM packages.** RevenueCat, Firebase Analytics, Lottie, Alamofire, etc. all have first-party equivalents good enough for most apps. Fewer deps = smaller binary, faster builds, no supply-chain risk, no privacy-manifest surprises.
- **Every framework that touches user data needs an `Info.plist` usage-description string** (or an entitlement). Missing it is a runtime crash the moment the API is used — not a compile error. The specific keys are listed per section.
- **Import the framework and its SwiftUI companion when one exists** (e.g. `import MapKit` gives you `Map`; `import StoreKit` gives you `SubscriptionStoreView`/`StoreView`).
- **Do capability checks before hardware-dependent APIs** (`CHHapticEngine.capabilitiesForHardware().supportsHaptics`, `HKHealthStore.isHealthDataAvailable()`, `GKLocalPlayer.local.isAuthenticated`). Simulators and older/cheaper devices lie.
- **Never block the main actor.** Long queries, audio-graph setup, and StoreKit calls belong in `Task {}` or `async` functions.
- **Verify APIs against the deployment target.** Several SwiftUI conveniences (e.g. `GameCenterView`, Control widgets) shipped *after* iOS 17. Availability call-outs below flag these.

---

## StoreKit 2 — In-App Purchase & Subscriptions

**Use it when:** you sell anything — consumables, non-consumables, or auto-renewable subscriptions. Replaces callback-based StoreKit 1 entirely.

**Start from:** `Product` (fetch + purchase) and `Transaction` (entitlements + history). No server strictly required — signatures are verified on-device via `VerificationResult`.

### The three things you must do

1. **Load products by ID** (IDs come from App Store Connect):

```swift
import StoreKit

let productIDs = ["com.app.pro.monthly", "com.app.pro.yearly", "com.app.coins.100"]
let products = try await Product.products(for: productIDs)   // async throws
```

2. **Purchase, then verify and finish the transaction:**

```swift
func purchase(_ product: Product) async throws -> Transaction? {
    let result = try await product.purchase()
    switch result {
    case .success(let verification):
        let transaction = try checkVerified(verification)
        await transaction.finish()          // REQUIRED — unfinished txns replay forever
        return transaction
    case .userCancelled, .pending:
        return nil
    @unknown default:
        return nil
    }
}

func checkVerified<T>(_ result: VerificationResult<T>) throws -> T {
    switch result {
    case .unverified(_, let error): throw error   // signature failed — do NOT grant
    case .verified(let safe):       return safe
    }
}
```

3. **Listen for `Transaction.updates` from app launch** — the single most-missed requirement. It catches renewals, Ask-to-Buy approvals, refunds, and purchases made on other devices.

```swift
// Start this in your App init / a top-level task and keep it alive for the app's lifetime.
func observeTransactions() -> Task<Void, Never> {
    Task.detached {
        for await update in Transaction.updates {
            guard case .verified(let transaction) = update else { continue }
            await grantEntitlement(for: transaction)   // your unlock logic
            await transaction.finish()
        }
    }
}
```

### Checking what the user currently owns

Use `Transaction.currentEntitlements` (an async sequence). **iOS 18.4+ note:** the per-product `Transaction.currentEntitlement(for:)` is deprecated in favor of `Transaction.currentEntitlements(for:)`, because a user can hold multiple entitling transactions (e.g. own it *and* have Family Sharing access).

```swift
func hasActiveSubscription() async -> Bool {
    for await result in Transaction.currentEntitlements {
        guard case .verified(let transaction) = result else { continue }
        if transaction.productType == .autoRenewable && transaction.revocationDate == nil {
            return true
        }
    }
    return false
}
```

```swift
// groupID = the subscription group configured in App Store Connect
let statuses = try await Product.SubscriptionInfo.status(for: subscriptionGroupID)
for status in statuses {

    let willAutoRenew = renewalInfo.willAutoRenew   // false => user cancelled, still in period
```

Architecturally I'd set this up as one Xcode project with two build targets (Waypoint app, WaypointWidget extension) plus one local Swift Package, WaypointKit, that both targets import. WaypointKit holds everything that must not visually or behaviorally drift between the app and the widget/Live Activity: the SwiftData model schema, Theme.swift, the shared component set that both surfaces render (DemoStampBadge, CategoryPin, the Ledger Numeral text style), and the plain services (StopReorderService, SettlementEngine, CalendarExportService, DemoSeeder, ActiveTripResolver). The app target owns everything screen-specific: TripSwitcher, DayView (with its MapKit pane), StopDetail, Travelers/Expenses/SettleUp, Packing, CalendarExportSummarySheet, Settings. The widget target owns NextStopWidget's TimelineProvider and the ActivityConfiguration for the Live Activity, both thin — they read WaypointKit models through the App Group–backed ModelContainer and render WaypointKit's shared components, they don't reimplement any presentation logic. I'd flag one real risk in this plan up front: local SPM packages containing @Model types imported by two different app targets is a workable but not bulletproof Xcode configuration — schema-registration or module-visibility issues are the kind of thing that can eat a day of setup pain. If that friction shows up early, the fallback is a shared-sources file group added to both targets instead of a true package; the important invariant is "one copy of the model/theme/component code," not the specific packaging mechanism.

On the schema itself: Trip (id: UUID, name, startDate, endDate, isDemo: Bool, createdAt, days: [Day] relationship, travelers: [Traveler], expenses: [Expense], packingItems: [PackingItem]) with days/travelers/expenses/packingItems all cascade-delete since none of them have a legitimate life outside their trip. Day (id: UUID, date: Date, trip: Trip, stops: [Stop]) is a real persisted row per calendar day of the trip, created eagerly when a trip is created or its range extended, and only removable via the shrink-guard flow that already blocks deletion when stops exist. Stop (id: UUID, day: Day — required, never optional, that's the invariant the whole atomic-move guarantee rests on — sortIndex: Int, name, address, latitude: Double?, longitude: Double?, startTime: Date?, endTime: Date?, notes, category: StopCategory, isCheckedOff: Bool, calendarEventIdentifier: String?). Traveler (id: UUID, trip: Trip, name). Expense (id: UUID, trip: Trip, amountCents: Int — the persisted source of truth is the integer, with a computed `amount: Decimal` accessor for display/entry so we never store two representations that could drift — payer: Traveler, date: Date, splitMethod: SplitMethod, notes: String?, splits: [ExpenseSplit] cascade). ExpenseSplit (id: UUID, expense: Expense, traveler: Traveler, shareCents: Int). PackingItem (id: UUID, trip: Trip, name, isPacked: Bool, sortIndex: Int). PackingTemplate/PackingTemplateItem mirror that shape for the should-have reuse feature. Storing money as Int cents at rest, not just computing in cents transiently, is a small but real upgrade from what was implied before — it means the sum-identity assertion can run as a stored-data integrity check at any time, not just right after a computation.

One gap nobody has closed yet and that I think the spec needs to close now, in the spirit of the Red Team ask: deleting a Traveler who already has expense involvement is completely unaddressed. Expense.payer is a required relationship and ExpenseSplit.traveler is required — if someone deletes a traveler mid-trip today, either SwiftData throws on the dangling required reference or (worse, if we're not careful with delete rules) it cascades and silently deletes ExpenseSplit rows, quietly changing a real expense's split from "3 people" to "2 people" after the fact with no record anything changed. That's the exact same failure family as the day-shrink-orphan problem this project already treats as top priority, just on the traveler axis instead of the stop axis, and it's currently unguarded. I'm proposing we lock the same pattern here: deleting a traveler who is a payer or split participant on any expense is blocked, with the UI surfacing exactly which expenses reference them, mirroring [REDACTED:high_entropy] exactly. A TravelerDeletionGuard service function closes this.

For persistence, I'd set up the ModelContainer with an explicit versioned Schema/SchemaMigrationPlan from day one — WaypointSchemaV1 today, even though it's the only version — rather than an unversioned container. This build is explicitly sequenced across multiple slices (core first, then packing templates/calendar/iPad, then Live Activity/widget/StoreKit fields), and every one of those later slices is going to want to add a field or a new model. Doing that against an unversioned schema means a destructive reinstall or a manual migration crisis later; doing it against a versioned plan from the start costs nothing now and saves real pain in three phases. Configuration is one ModelConfiguration with `cloudKitDatabase: .none` (explicit, not just absent) and `groupContainer: .identifier("group.<bundle>.waypoint")`, used by both the app and the widget extension, which is also where the #if DEBUG current-date hook's UserDefaults suite lives.

On concurrency, I want to name a boundary that's easy to get wrong: SwiftData's PersistentModel objects are tied to the ModelContext that fetched them and are not something you casually hand across an `await` boundary into EventKit/MapKit async calls. StopReorderService and SettlementEngine stay fully synchronous, main-actor, operating directly on model objects passed a ModelContext — there's no real async work in either, and keeping them synchronous keeps the atomic-save-then-animate sequencing simple. CalendarExportService and MKDirections calls are genuinely async, so they extract plain Sendable DTOs (stop name/address/time window/existing event id) from the model objects before crossing into the async call, then apply the result back on the main actor afterward — never hold a live model reference across an awaited system call.

On performance, since trip/day/stop counts here are small by construction (a demo or real trip is dozens of stops at most), I'd deliberately not reach for `@Query` with relationship-traversing `#Predicate`s — fetch the Trip, read `trip.days` and `day.stops` directly, sort by `sortIndex`/`date` in plain Swift. Where I would spend effort: give the widget a real `widgetURL`/deep link (`waypoint://trip/<id>/day/<id>`) so tapping "next stop" on the home screen actually opens that day, since a widget that doesn't deep-link anywhere is a widget nobody trusts — this isn't new scope, it's the baseline of the already-committed widget feature actually working.

Testing strategy carries forward what's locked (in-memory ModelContainer XCTest for SettlementEngine and StopReorderService, Move-to-driven repeated cross-day stress test, manual verification of the actual finger-drag) and adds the traveler-deletion guard as its own adversarial test case, plus one perf sanity check: seed a stress trip (30 days × 10 stops, 8 travelers, 40 expenses) purely in the test target and confirm the day view's data access stays snappy and the settlement engine's minimum-transaction result is still correct at that scale, not just at the 5-traveler demo scale.
